final_answer:
>>> Rayleigh scattering occurs when light interacts with particles much smaller than its wavelength, such as gas molecules in Earth's atmosphere. During the day, sunlight (white light) enters the atmosphere and scatters across all directions. Shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) scatter more intensely than longer wavelengths (red/orange) because the scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength ($ I \propto 1/\lambda^4 $). This is why the sky appears blue—blue light is scattered in all directions, filling the sky with blue hues.  

>>> At sunset, sunlight travels through a much longer path in the atmosphere compared to midday. Along this extended path, most of the blue and violet light is scattered away, leaving predominantly red and orange wavelengths to reach the observer. The direct sunlight that reaches the horizon appears red because the shorter wavelengths have been filtered out. Additionally, the scattered blue light is already dispersed in earlier layers of the atmosphere, reducing its dominance in the line of sight. This combination of increased scattering and wavelength filtering explains the red/orange hues of sunsets.
